rv.q: The wait at last is over and now, 28 years after the death of Francis Albert Sinatra, the legend lives again in the West End.
This will be too 'authorised' and synthetic for people – like me – who want to get behind those sly blue eyes.
Sinatra: The Musical is a turbulent experience, boasting more than 20 Sinatra hits and sleek, glossy staging, but is let down by poor writing that never quite gets under the legendary artist’s skin.
Sinatra the Musical, which takes the story up to the From Here to Eternity comeback in 1953, is a similarly erratic affair.

But the trouble is that the format doesn’t allow for in-depth exploration of these issues, resulting in a somewhat superficial account of events — curiously anodyne too, given the extraordinary details of Sinatra’s life.
But a reluctance to embrace too much darkness lends a sense that things just happen to our hero.
But despite polished performances all round and serious brass band umph, it’s a humdrum affair that fails to fully capture Sinatra’s remarkable achievements or the glamour of Hollywood’s glitterati.
The songs are great but this compromised bio-musical tries to make Frank Sinatra seem as boring as humanly possible
But for all the unarguable style that the English performer Joel Harper-Jackson brings to “Ol’ Blue Eyes,” there’s no getting around the plodding, pro forma quality of the show itself.
Teams of archaeologists could labour for decades without unearthing the point of this show.
Sinatra: The Musical is the real thing.
Sinatra the Musical is a show that really is a masterclass in everything that a West End show should be.
Sinatra maintains a lively pace from the outset with Joel Harper-Jackson in the title role onstage virtually throughout.
Sinatra The Musical ultimately succeeds, leaving you with a renewed appreciation for the music that made Frank Sinatra an enduring icon.
Dazzling Sinatra the Musical is in the intimate Aldwych, this personal story so much better here than in a large arena.
It’s a slickly produced one that’s high in entertainment value and features tremendous big-band virtuosity.
This show erases the dark side and treats him like an all-American charmer whose triumph is inevitable.
Dramatically inert but musically magnificent, this is a solid tribute to a singular talent, and will undoubtedly prove a glamorous summer hit.
Despite all that, and factoring in a running time of close to three hours, the man and his motivations remain frustratingly opaque.
Like much that is sanitised and simplified for a mass market, Sinatra The Musical flattens a complex life, scatters glitter liberally around it and sends its public away happy, toes tapping.
Joel Harper-Jackson delivers a star turn, proving what a remarkable leading man he is in what is easily a career-best performance.
Overall this new biographical show of Sinatra is an impressive addition to the West End.
There's a really sharp, sensitive play in there, unwritten, which haunted my imagination all through this big, blasting, powerhouse show.
This production sadly felt a little bit too ‘corny’ and repetitive in places, plus lacked a real sense of depth, characterisation and charisma.

The principal cast, however, ensures that Sinatra The Musical earns its three-star rating, not only through the quality of their vocals but by bringing emotional depth to characters who are not always well served by DiPietro's book.
If you are coming here curious to learn more about the man and the legend, Joe DiPietro’s book comes up a little short.
Those curious enough to attend a jukebox musical for a man who died 28 years ago will find a book that simplifies a complicated artist and human being, but has some striking moments.
For all its many faults, there are some saving graces in the show.
The production’s greatest achievement is making someone this famous feel unexpectedly real.
Have no doubt, Sinatra the Musical is uplifting and full of joy, a proper night out on the tiles, and I suspect it won’t just be Sinatra fans who enjoy this heartwarming show.
The production belongs to Joel Harper-Jackson.
Joel Harper-Jackson does a remarkable job with the well-known songs but the book lets him down and reduces this musical to a collection of songs rather than something more iconic and emotional.

cn.t: Critics find Sinatra The Musical a slick but superficial jukebox show elevated by Joel Harper-Jackson's stunning vocals and a superb live band, yet hampered by a flat, airbrushed book that never captures the icon's complexity or emotional depth.
